artifact: external OSS audit summary (licence / dependency / supply-chain / reproducibility)

projects.name: SciTrends
projects.type: research artefact: Jupyter notebooks + committed derived CSV/Parquet features; no package, service or CLI
projects.licence: NO LICENCE FILE - repository, companion webapp repo and committed data are all unlicensed. Paper is CC BY-NC-ND.
projects.licence_verdict: no confirmed code licence - method-only borrowing allowed, code reuse forbidden
projects.core_tech: Python/Jupyter; CatBoost + RidgeCV + sentence-transformers; sklearn TimeSeriesSplit(30); pandas
projects.core_method: topic popularity = 100000 * topic_pubs(year) / total_medline_pubs(year); target = popularity(t+5) or 100*(popularity(t+5)-popularity(t-5))/popularity(t); features include review:research ratios, patent counts/fracs, lags; CatBoost with topic categorical + topic-name embeddings; step-forward 30-fold CV over year-sorted rows
projects.data_deps: in-repo derived tables (trends_v6.csv.gz 533 KB et al, all <1 MB); upstream PubMed-by-Year scrape (unpinned hobby site) and USPTO PatentsView (API-key gated; released call contains a masked 'secret_url')
projects.accessible_now_detail: code and all modelling data are public and were fetched; raw data regeneration is not possible (patents gated behind key, PubMed series comes from an unpinned third-party scrape)
projects.local_run_result: method-logic reproduction SUCCEEDED: independent 274 s run, exit 0, on the authors' released 533,335-byte trends_v6.csv.gz (sha256 fbd32b59...). 4,175 rows / 123 topics / 1979-2015. Lag baseline reproduces Table 1 EXACTLY on four metrics for two target definitions: level R2 0.9732 / MAE 113.806 / medAE 44.378 / RMSE 229.128 vs paper 0.973 / 113.80 / 44.37 / 229.12; percent-delta R2 0.0039 / MAE 115.419 / medAE 83.377 / RMSE 289.980 vs paper 0.004 / 115.42 / 83.38 / 289.98. CatBoost and sentence-transformers unavailable, so boosting rows were run with a substituted sklearn HistGradientBoostingRegressor (level R2 0.9770, pct R2 0.1058) and embedding rows were not run.
projects.overlap_with_medradar: LOW-to-MODERATE and feature-level only: MedRadar already has OpenAlex annual publication counts and growth features (medradar/intelligence/features/publication_features.py) but explicitly normalises within-company only ('not a share of industry output', line 26) and collects NO review/research split. SciTrends supplies exactly those two definitions. Its validation protocol is weaker than MedRadar's own point-in-time/purged machinery and must not be adopted.
methods_to_migrate: normalised popularity: popularity(company, year) = 100000 * pubs(company, year) / total_pubs(field, year) - repairs the documented within-company-only limitation of publication_features.py
review : research decomposition of publication counts (ratio and difference as a directional feature) - currently entirely absent from MedRadar
patent share of annual patent output as a leading indicator (definition only; cannot be evaluated until the USPTO key exists)
limitations: notebooks only: no package, CLI, tests, CI, versioning
no licence on code or committed data
no pinned environment; released notebooks no longer run on current pandas (infer_datetime_format and mode.use_inf_as_na both removed)
data generation not reproducible: PatentsView key-gated with the released URL masked, PubMed-by-Year is an unpinned scrape
125 hand-picked biomedical topics, not a device/drug taxonomy
level-target skill is dominated by autocorrelation (persistence R2 0.969 with no model)
leakage_risks: topic survivorship: topics were selected in 2022 for present-day activity, so backtests condition on survival
level-target illusion: popularity(t+5) approx popularity(t); R2 0.97+ is autocorrelation, not forecast skill
label mislabelling: the delta target spans t-5 to t+5 (10 years) normalised by popularity(t), not a 5-year change as the paper prose suggests
committed feature table was computed once over full history and is not point-in-time
known-topic advantage disappears under topic-level splits (paper Table 2: R2 0.86 vs 0.98)
popularity normaliser itself drifts with NLM indexing policy
projects.decision_reason: The licence forbids reusing any code or data file (no la licence file exists anywhere, and the paper is NC-ND), but an independent implementation of the method is permitted and the reproduction shows it is trustworthy: my rebuild of the lag baseline matches Table 1 to the last reported digit on four metrics for two independent target definitions. The two feature definitions (output-normalised popularity, review:research ratio) target weaknesses MedRadar's own source documents, so the method is worth adapting under attribution - while its validation protocol, models, embeddings and published effect sizes should not be imported.

projects.name: PubTrends
projects.type: production web service: Flask + Celery + PostgreSQL/pgvector + Redis + Faiss + Kotlin loader + Bokeh/HoloViews UI
projects.licence: Apache License 2.0 - LICENSE.txt, 11316 bytes, canonical text, 'Copyright 2022 JetBrains Research.'
projects.core_tech: Python 3.12 + Kotlin; Flask, Celery, PostgreSQL 17 + pgvector, Redis 7.4.2, gensim Word2Vec (node2vec), scikit-learn, transformers/ONNX, faiss-cpu, bokeh/holoviews
projects.core_method: bibliometric graph (co-citation + bibliographic coupling + citation + hybrid text similarity) with composite weight 10*co + 3*bc + 1*cit + 20*text; 50-NN sparsification; node2vec (p=5, q=2, walk 30, 50 walks, dim 64); PCA at 0.9 variance; AgglomerativeClustering under 5000 papers else KMeans; clusters described by cosine of cluster frequency vectors to one-hot weighted by log1p(total); citation analytics (top cited, per-year absolute max gain, per-year relative gain)
projects.install_method: uv sync from pyproject.toml inside Dockerfile (python:3.10-slim) or docker-compose (4 variants); requires a populated PostgreSQL 17 + pgvector
projects.data_deps: PubMed XML baseline/update packs via NCBI FTP (~40M papers / 450M citations) or Semantic Scholar Open Corpus (170M papers / 600M citations); PostgreSQL 17 + pgvector + Redis + Faiss; docs recommend 8 GB effective_cache_size and -m 32G for pgvector
projects.accessible_now_detail: all 267 source blobs are public and were fetched; the DATA is not accessible here - terabyte-class corpora plus a forbidden service stack
projects.local_run_result: algorithm reimplementation SUCCEEDED: independent pure-Python port, exit 0, 0.04 s, 9/9 checks passed, no database and no service. Verified node2vec p/q transition probabilities analytically and against 200k sampled walks, the 10/3/1/20 similarity formula, k-NN invariants, cluster relabelling, one-hot-cosine topic description, and citation-gain analytics. Two upstream defects measured: sparse_graph exceeds its k degree cap (18 nodes over k=5, max degree 7), and the relative 'hot paper' gain exceeds 1.0 in a paper's first citation year (measured 10.0).
projects.overlap_with_medradar: LOW: overlaps MedRadar's bibliographic INPUTS (OpenAlex publication counts via medradar/intelligence/sources/publications.py, graph_context, tkg bitemporal store) but not its purpose. PubTrends has no train/test split, no future target and no accuracy metric, so it cannot contribute to the forecasting lane. MedRadar's point-in-time discipline is materially stricter. Genuine gap it could fill: clustering/labelling a paper set into named topics - not currently needed because MedRadar uses a curated track taxonomy.
methods_to_migrate: topic description by cosine of cluster frequency vector to one-hot, weighted by log1p(total) - ~40 lines, useful only if a literature-clustering feature is ever built
composite multi-source paper-similarity weighting (10/3/1/20) as a reference schema - ~10 lines
greedy k-NN graph sparsification - ~20 lines, but fix the degree-cap defect rather than replicate it
limitations: an exploration/dashboard product, not a predictive method: no target, no split, no score anywhere in ~12.8k LOC
requires PostgreSQL + pgvector + Redis + Celery + Faiss; full stack deployment forbidden by the audit brief
datasets are terabyte-scale and were not downloaded
48 of 52 Python dependencies unpinned, so the analysis stack is not reproducible in detail
all algorithm constants are hardcoded with no calibration or sensitivity evidence in the repo
internal metadata inconsistency: version.py 'development' vs pyproject 1.0.0; python:3.10 image vs requires-python ==3.12.*
leakage_risks: no point-in-time discipline: a result set is clustered using all returned papers, including papers published after the reasoning date, so historical 'emerging area' claims leak the future
cumulative citation counts are contemporaneous and are not leading indicators
the relative-gain 'hot paper' metric is biased toward papers in their first citation year (denominator guard 0->1; measured value 10.0 for a 10-citation first year)
cluster identity is not stable across queries or years, so 'topic X grew' is not a defined statement
KMeans is called without random_state (unlike node2vec's seed=42), so clusters are non-deterministic above 5000 papers
projects.decision_reason: Licence is genuinely clean (Apache-2.0, no vendored code, no sublicensing conflict), so reuse would be legally easy - but there is nothing to adopt for a forecasting pipeline: PubTrends is a snapshot literature explorer with no temporal model, no train/test protocol and no predictive metric, and its predict_analyzer is a random-sample demo. Reuse would mean standing up Postgres + pgvector + Redis + Celery + Faiss and loading terabyte-scale corpora to obtain ~150 lines of clustering utility, which the brief explicitly forbids and which MedRadar's curated track taxonomy does not currently need. The clean licence and good engineering are recorded so a future clustering feature can start from a known reference.

program_level_findings: Neither repository vendors third-party code, so neither carries a sublicensing conflict.
The two projects are licence opposites: SciTrends has no licence at all (code reuse forbidden), PubTrends has a clean Apache-2.0 (reuse permitted). Decision must not be driven by licence alone.

Only PubTrends has supply-chain hazards worth registering: a pip dependency installed from a GitHub release URL with no hash, a third-party torch index, a Docker build that pipes a remote script to sh, a pickle cache without integrity checks, a hardcoded default SECURITY_PASSWORD_SALT, committed default database/admin credentials, and an empty .env.example.
Neither repository contains a requirements.txt that installs from a git+ URL; the closest analogue is PubTrends' direct wheel URL for en-core-web-sm.
Only SciTrends' method was numerically verifiable, and it verified exactly - but only on the authors' pre-derived table, which is derived data with no licence.
